meaning: Centers on a topic around which there is debate, conflict or discussion: “over ...”, “surrounding ...”. Used for issues where several sides disagree.
connection: Noun + をめぐって／をめぐり／をめぐる + noun

senses.label: Over / surrounding
senses.meaning: Several parties argue or act over a certain issue: “over ...”, “surrounding ...”. The second half is usually a verb like 「議論する」, 「対立する」, 「争う」 or 「もめる」. It implies that opinions are divided.
senses.connection: Noun + をめぐって／をめぐり (the latter mid-sentence in writing)
examples: Residents are divided over the construction of the new airport.
The brothers are fighting over the inheritance.
Heated debate continued in the Diet over the bill.

senses.label: Modifying a noun
senses.meaning: 「〜をめぐる + noun」 modifies the following noun: “the (issue, dispute, incident) surrounding ...”. Very common in news headlines and reports.
senses.connection: Noun + をめぐる／をめぐっての + noun (問題・議論・争い・対立, etc.)
examples: Territorial disputes are not easily resolved.
Criticism of the prime minister's remarks poured in.

notes: The second half must be something several parties take part in: debate, opposition, investigation, negotiation. Actions by one person on their own can't be used: ✕「この本をめぐって感想を書いた」→ ○「この本について感想を書いた」.
To simply explain or present a topic, use 「について」: ✕「日本の文化をめぐって発表します」→ ○「日本の文化について発表します」. With 「をめぐって」, listeners will assume the topic is controversial.
To modify a noun, use 「をめぐる」 or 「をめぐっての」; it can't connect to a noun directly: ✕「領土をめぐって問題」→ ○「領土をめぐる問題」.
It carries a tone of dispute or opposition. Saying about a colleague or client 「〜をめぐってもめている」 makes the situation sound serious; for a peaceful discussion, say 「〜について話し合っている」.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: News reports often use 「〜をめぐる」 for controversial topics.
daily.example: The debate over raising the consumption tax continues.

daily.title: A family argument
daily.description: Telling a friend that your family argued about something.
daily.example: We had a family fight over where to go on our weekend trip.

work.title: Meeting minutes
work.description: Summarizing the main points of disagreement in meeting notes.
work.example: Each department gave its opinion on how the budget should be allocated.

work.title: News report
work.description: A reporter covers an investigation or dispute surrounding an incident.
work.example: Police are investigating the cause of the accident.

etymology: 「めぐる」 is written 「巡る・廻る」 and originally means “to go around, to circle”. From “circling around something” it came to mean “(debate, etc.) centering on an issue”.

similar.title: 〜について
similar.explanation: 「〜について」 only marks the topic (“about ...”), and the second half can be any action such as reading, writing or speaking; 「〜をめぐって」 stresses that several sides argue or clash over the topic. 「環境問題について調べる」 can't be changed to 「をめぐって」.

similar.title: 〜に関して・〜に関する
similar.explanation: A slightly more formal version of 「について」; it likewise just marks a related topic and carries no sense of opposing views. When reporting a dispute or conflict, 「〜をめぐる」 is the better fit.

similar.title: 〜を中心に
similar.explanation: Both evoke the image of “centering on something.” 「〜を中心に」 means activity develops with a person or thing as its core or focus (「若者を中心に人気がある」), with no hint of argument; the “center” of 「〜をめぐって」 is the point of contention.

formation: Built from the case particle 「を」 plus the te-form of the verb 「めぐる」 (written 「巡る」, “to go around, circle”). 「を」 marks the center that is circled, and 「めぐって」 means “circling around it.” Project the image of many people milling around one center onto an abstract level and you get “several sides argue or clash over an issue.” Because it is “many people going around,” the second half is always an action involving several parties, and it often carries a note of conflict or dispute. The continuative form 「めぐり」 is more literary for a mid-sentence pause, and the attributive form 「めぐる」 modifies a noun, which neatly matches the forms the pattern takes.

meaning: One action serves two purposes or functions at once: “also as ...”, “combined with ...”. Killing two birds with one stone.
connection: Noun + を兼ねて／も兼ねて; Noun 1 + を兼ねた + Noun 2

senses.label: Doubling as a purpose
senses.meaning: While doing one thing, you also achieve another purpose: “partly as ...”, “while also ...”. The noun before it is the extra purpose. 「〜も兼ねて」 means “also partly for ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + を兼ねて／も兼ねて + action (運動・勉強・下見・気分転換・挨拶, etc.)
examples: I walk to work every morning, partly for the exercise.
We ate near the venue, which also let us check out the place.
Why don't we take a little walk? It'll be a nice change of pace, too.

senses.label: Serving two functions
senses.meaning: 「AをかねたB」 means one thing has two functions or uses at once: “a B that doubles as A”.
senses.connection: Noun 1 + を兼ねた + Noun 2 (書斎を兼ねた寝室・趣味と実益を兼ねた仕事, etc.)
examples: I work in a bedroom that doubles as a study.
This is a job that combines my hobby with a way to earn money.

notes: It looks like 「〜かねる」 (“hard to ...”) and 「〜かねない」 (“might ...”) but is quite different in meaning. When you see 「動詞ます形＋かねる」 as in 「お答えしかねます」 or 「事故になりかねない」, don't read it as “doubling”; the meaning is completely different.
It attaches to nouns, not directly to verbs: ✕「運動するを兼ねて」→ ○「運動を兼ねて」.
When visiting a client or a superior, put only purposes related to them before 「を兼ねて」 (「ご挨拶を兼ねて」, 「お礼を兼ねて」). Saying 「買い物を兼ねて伺いました」 amounts to “I dropped by on the way,” which is very rude.
In 「AをかねたB」, B is the main function and A the secondary one: 「書斎を兼ねた寝室」 is “a bedroom that doubles as a study,” so the bedroom is the main thing; the order can't be reversed.

daily.title: Going out to shop
daily.description: Telling your family you'll pop out to shop and take a walk on the way.
daily.example: I'm going to the convenience store. It'll be a nice walk, too.

daily.title: Learning a language
daily.description: A friend asks why you watch foreign dramas. You say it's also for study.
daily.example: I watch Japanese dramas without subtitles, partly as study.

daily.title: Showing a room
daily.description: Explaining what a room is for to a visiting friend.
daily.example: This is the living room. It doubles as a guest room.

work.title: Business visit
work.description: Explaining that your visit to a client is also to say hello.
work.example: I'd like to visit you once, partly to introduce myself in person.

work.title: Business trip plans
work.description: Telling your boss you'll make an inspection during the trip.
work.example: While I'm on the business trip, I'll also tour the local factory.

etymology: 「兼ねる」 originally means “to hold two roles at once, to combine”. 「を兼ねて」 is its te-form: “while doing the main thing, it also serves as ...”.

similar.title: 〜ついでに
similar.explanation: 「〜ついでに」 means “taking the opportunity of doing A, also do B,” where B is an impromptu addition (「買い物のついでに郵便局に寄る」); 「〜を兼ねて」 means one action carries two purposes from the start, usually planned in advance (「運動を兼ねて歩いて通勤する」).

similar.title: 〜がてら
similar.explanation: 「〜がてら」 mostly follows nouns like 「散歩」 or 「買い物」, and the second half is usually a movement verb such as 「行く」 or 「寄る」 (「散歩がてら本屋に寄る」); it can't modify a noun either. 「〜を兼ねて」 has no restriction on the type of action and also allows 「〜を兼ねた部屋」.

similar.title: 〜かたがた
similar.explanation: 「〜かたがた」 is literary, used mainly in letters and business courtesies after nouns like 「お礼」, 「ご挨拶」 or 「ご報告」, with a second half such as 「伺う」 or 「お願いする」 (「お礼かたがたご挨拶に伺います」). 「〜を兼ねて」 has no such limits and is common in everyday speech too.

formation: Built from the case particle 「を」 plus the te-form of the verb 「兼ねる」. 「兼ねる」 originally means “one thing carries two roles,” as in 「社長が会長を兼ねる」 (the president doubles as chairman). Literally, 「Aを兼ねてB」 is “while doing B, also take on A”: B is the main activity and A is the side purpose handled along the way, hence the “two birds with one stone” feel. The attributive 「Aを兼ねたB」 means “a B that also serves as A,” again with B primary and A secondary. And because 「兼ねる」 means “to hold a role as well,” only nouns can come before it.

meaning: After passing through a place, a period of time, or a stage or procedure, you reach the next step: “via ...”, “after ...”.
connection: Noun + を経て／を経た + noun

senses.label: Via a place
senses.meaning: Going through a place on the way to a destination: “via ...”, “by way of ...”. Mostly used to describe transport and routes.
senses.connection: Place noun + を経て + destination へ／に
examples: The plane flies to Singapore via Hong Kong.
I went by Shinkansen to Fukuoka, by way of Osaka.

senses.label: After a period of time
senses.meaning: After a span of time has passed, things have changed: “after ...”, “over ...”. Often used with 「年月」, 「歳月」 or 「〜年」. Very literary.
senses.connection: Time noun + を経て (十年・長い年月・歳月, etc.)
examples: After ten years, the bridge was finally completed.
Buildings that have stood for many years have a special charm.

senses.label: Through a procedure
senses.meaning: Only after going through a stage, procedure or experience do you move to the next step: “after (going through) ...”. Common for formal processes like reviews, debates and exams.
senses.connection: Noun + を経て (審査・議論・試験・手続き・苦労, etc.)
examples: After a rigorous selection process, his work was chosen.
The law was passed after debate in the Diet.
This plan was decided without going through the committee.

notes: 「経て」 is read 「へて」. The 「経つ」 in 「十年が経って」 is read 「たつ」, means time passing, and takes 「が」; don't say ✕「十年を経って」 or read 「を経て」 as 「たって」.
It means passing through a place, stage or period before the next step; it can't mean “by means of”: ✕「インターネットを経て申し込む」→ ○「インターネットを通じて申し込む」.
It is literary. When describing routes in speech, 「〜経由で」 or 「〜を通って」 are more common: 「香港経由でシンガポールへ行く」.

daily.title: Describing a trip
daily.description: Telling a friend about your travel route.
daily.example: I traveled by train to Rome, by way of Paris.

daily.title: Telling your story
daily.description: Talking about how you achieved your dream after many setbacks.
daily.example: After failing again and again, I finally got my own shop.

work.title: Company announcement
work.description: An announcement explains that a personnel decision went through the proper process.
work.example: With the approval of the board of directors, a new president has been chosen.

work.title: Academic paper
work.description: Stating that research results were peer-reviewed.
work.example: This paper was published after peer review.

etymology: 「経る」 is an old verb meaning “to pass through (a place), to go through (time)”. The kanji 「経」 carries the idea of passing or going through, as in 「経由」 (“via”) and 「経験」 (“experience”).

similar.title: 〜を通じて・〜を通して
similar.explanation: 「〜を通じて」 stresses “through ... as a medium or channel” (「友人を通じて知り合う」) or “throughout the whole period”; 「〜を経て」 stresses that you finish this stage before moving on to the next, i.e. the order of steps.

similar.title: 〜末(に)
similar.explanation: 「〜末(に)」 means arriving at a result after long effort or agonizing (「悩んだ末に決めた」), stressing the hardship of the process; 「〜を経て」 merely states the stages or time passed, without that emotional coloring.

similar.title: 〜にわたって
similar.explanation: Both can go with time expressions. 「十年にわたって」 means continuing for a full ten years, looking at the span; 「十年を経て」 means after ten years had passed, looking at the result afterward.

formation: Built from the case particle 「を」 plus the te-form of the classical verb 「経る」 (read 「へる」, “to pass through, undergo”). The 「を」 here is the 「を」 of movement through a place (as in 「公園を通る」), so 「Aを経て」 literally means “passing through A.” Extend that spatial “passing through a point” to time and procedure and you get “after a span of years” or “after passing a review.” The te-form links the passage to what follows: “finish this stretch A, then arrive at B,” so the second half is always the next stage or the final result.

meaning: You meant to do something, but for some reason it never happened, and now it's over. Carries a sense of regret: “never got to ...”.
connection: Verb nai-form (drop ない) + ずじまい (する → せずじまい)

senses.label: Never got to do it
senses.meaning: Something you wanted or ought to do ended up never getting done: “in the end, never ...”, “never managed to ...”. Carries regret. Often used with 「結局」 or 「とうとう」.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ずじまいだ／ずじまいだった／ずじまいに終わる
examples: In the end, I never got to hear how she really felt.
I finally bought that book, but I've been too busy and never read it.
The plan ended without ever being carried out.

senses.label: Linking / modifying
senses.meaning: 「〜ずじまいで」 means that, without having done something, the next thing happened. 「〜ずじまいの + noun」 modifies a noun: “the ... that never got done”.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ずじまいで + clause; ずじまいの + noun
examples: I moved away without ever going to that shop even once.
The words I never said still linger in my heart.

notes: Used only for things you meant or ought to do but never managed, with a sense of regret; it can't be used for things you didn't want to do anyway: ✕「嫌いな納豆は食べずじまいだった」→ ○「嫌いな納豆は結局食べなかった」.
「する」 becomes 「せずじまい」, not ✕「しずじまい」; 「来る」 becomes 「来ずじまい(こずじまい)」.
It looks back on something already settled; don't use it while there is still a chance: ✕「まだ一週間あるが、行かずじまいだ」→ ○「まだ一週間あるが、まだ行っていない」.

daily.title: After a trip
daily.description: Telling a friend you didn't get to see a place you wanted to.
daily.example: Because of the rain, I never got to see Mt. Fuji.

daily.title: Losing touch with an old friend
daily.description: Looking back with regret that you never thanked someone.
daily.example: I never got to thank him, and then I couldn't see him anymore.

work.title: Project wrap-up
work.description: Stating in a report that a problem was never solved.
work.example: The investigation was called off with the cause still unknown.

etymology: 「じまい」 is the voiced form of 「しまい」 (「仕舞い」, “end”). 「ず」 is the classical negative auxiliary. Together they mean “ending in a state of not having done ...”. Also written 「ず仕舞い」.

similar.title: 〜まま
similar.explanation: 「〜ないまま」 means something happened while a certain thing was left undone (「一度も会わないまま別れた」), merely describing a state; 「〜ずじまい」 looks at “never got to do it even at the end,” with a stronger sense of regret and finality.

similar.title: 〜ことなく
similar.explanation: 「〜ことなく」 means “without doing ...,” often for positive persistence (「休むことなく働く」), with no regret; 「〜ずじまい」 is something you wanted to do but couldn't, a negative, regretful tone.

similar.title: 〜てしまう
similar.explanation: Related: 「じまい」 is the noun form of 「しまう(仕舞う)」. 「〜てしまう」 shows an action completed, or regret over doing something you shouldn't have; 「〜ずじまい」 means what you should have done ended up “not done.”

formation: Built from the classical negative auxiliary 「ず」 plus 「しまい(仕舞い)」, with 「しまい」 voiced to 「じまい」. 「しまい」 is the noun form of the verb 「しまう」 (written 「仕舞う」, “to put away, finish”) and means “the end, the close”; it shares its origin with 「〜てしまう」. Literally, 「〜ずじまい」 is “ending in a state of not having ...”: the matter has closed, but what you meant to do stayed in the “not done” state, hence “never managed to ... in the end.” 「しまう」 itself carries a sense of “finished, irreversible,” which is why the pattern comes with regret and is mostly used in the past tense.

meaning: You get by without having to do something you thought was necessary, or you avoid a bad outcome. Carries a sense of relief.
connection: Verb nai-form (drop ない) + ずに済む (する → せずに済む); Verb nai-form + で済む

senses.label: Don't have to
senses.meaning: Something you thought you'd have to do turned out to be unnecessary: “get by without ...”, “be spared ...”. Implies “that saved me trouble”.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ずに済む／ないで済む (済んだ・済みます)
examples: A friend drove me home, so I didn't need a taxi.
I could reach them by email, so I didn't have to go into the office.
If you live nearby, you won't have to ride packed trains.

senses.label: Avoiding a bad outcome
senses.meaning: Luckily, something unwanted didn't happen: “fortunately didn't ...”. The verb before it is usually something negative like 「けがをする」, 「大事になる」 or 「遅れる」.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ずに済んだ／ないで済んだ (often with 「おかげで」 or 「早めに」)
examples: Thanks to noticing it early, it didn't turn into anything serious.
I was wearing a seatbelt, so I didn't get hurt.

senses.label: Managing without
senses.meaning: 「〜ずに済ませる／〜ないで済ませる」 means finding a way to get by without doing something. It implies active arrangement.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ずに済ませる／ないで済ませる
examples: If possible, I'd like to get through this without surgery.
I skipped lunch.

notes: 「〜ずに済む」 and 「〜ずには済まない」 differ only by a 「は」 and a negative, and mean opposite things: 「謝らずに済んだ」 is “I didn't have to apologize,” while 「謝らずには済まない」 is “I can't get away without apologizing.”
「する」 becomes 「せずに済む」, not ✕「しずに済む」.
「名詞＋で済む」 means “it was settled with only this much cost”: 「軽いけがで済んだ」 is “got off with only a minor injury,” while 「けがをせずに済んだ」 is “wasn't injured at all”; the degree differs.
The transitive 「〜ずに済ませる」 means actively managing not to do something; telling a client 「確認せずに済ませました」 sounds like cutting corners, so use it carefully at work.

daily.title: The weather clears up
daily.description: You thought you'd need an umbrella, but the rain stopped.
daily.example: The rain stopped, so I didn't have to take an umbrella.

daily.title: At the doctor
daily.description: Telling your family it wasn't serious and you won't be hospitalized.
daily.example: It was just a mild cold, so I didn't have to stay in the hospital.

daily.title: Online shopping
daily.description: Telling a friend about the perks of shopping online.
daily.example: If you buy online, you don't have to carry heavy bags.

work.title: Reporting to your boss
work.description: Explaining that acting early avoided losses.
work.example: Because we responded early, we avoided a major loss.

work.title: Online meetings
work.description: A coworker says remote meetings saved a business trip.
work.example: Thanks to the online meeting, I didn't have to go on a business trip.

etymology: 「済む」 originally means “(a matter) to be settled, to be finished”. 「〜ずに済む」 literally means “the matter gets settled without doing ...”, hence “don't have to, be spared ...”.

similar.title: 〜て済む・〜ずに済む
similar.explanation: Related (both use 「済む」). 「〜て済む」 means “doing ... settles it” (「謝って済む問題ではない」), affirming the first half; 「〜ずに済む」 means “settling it without doing ....” One is solved at a small cost, the other lets you off completely.

similar.title: 〜なくてもいい
similar.explanation: 「〜なくてもいい」 gives permission or a judgment that something is “not necessary,” mostly beforehand (「明日は来なくてもいい」); 「〜ずに済む」 is mostly used afterward, with a sense of relief at having avoided something.

similar.title: 〜ことはない
similar.explanation: 「〜ことはない」 means “there's no need to ...,” mostly in comforting or advising the listener (「心配することはない」); 「〜ずに済む」 states that some circumstance spared you from doing something.

formation: Built from the negative form 「〜ず(に)／〜ないで」 plus the verb 「済む」. 「済む」 originally means “a matter is finished or settled,” as in 「用事が済む」. Literally, 「〜ずに済む」 is “the matter gets settled in a state of not doing ...”: something you thought you had to do, or that seemed bound to happen, turned out not to be necessary. Because it presupposes “it should have been done / would have happened,” it carries a “fortunately, thank goodness” feel. Swap the intransitive 「済む」 for the transitive 「済ませる」 and the speaker actively “manages to get things done without doing ....”

meaning: Follows a potential verb and strongly says “you just can't ...”, “it's impossible to ...”. Carries a negative, critical tone.
connection: Potential verb ta-form + ものではない (casual: 〜たもんじゃない)

senses.label: Simply can't
senses.meaning: Things are so bad that doing something is impossible: “you just can't ...”, “there's no way to ...”. A very low evaluation, showing the speaker's dissatisfaction or disgust.
senses.connection: Potential verb ta-form + ものではない／もんじゃない (食べられた・見られた・聞けた・読めた, etc.)
examples: Food this awful is simply inedible.
His handwriting is so messy it's impossible to read.
Such bad singing is just unbearable to listen to.

senses.label: Who knows what ...
senses.meaning: 「〜か分かったものではない」 means “who knows what/when ...”, “there's no telling ...”. It expresses worry or distrust about a bad outcome. Often used with question words like 「何を」, 「いつ」 or 「どこで」.
senses.connection: Question word ... + か分かったものではない／知れたものではない
examples: There's no telling what that person will come out with.
Driving like this, who knows when you'll cause an accident.

notes: What precedes must be the ta-form of a potential verb or 「分かる」: 「食べられたものではない」, 「何をするか分かったものではない」; a plain verb as in ✕「食べたものではない」 doesn't work.
The tone is strongly disparaging; commenting on someone's cooking or work, it amounts to “impossible to eat / watch,” so saying it to the person, or to a superior or client, is extremely rude.

It differs from 「〜ものではない」 (“shouldn't ...”) only by the potential form and 「た」, yet means something entirely different: 「人の悪口を言うものではない」 is “you shouldn't speak ill of others,” while 「聞けたものではない」 is “simply unbearable to listen to.”
「分かったものではない」 means “who knows, it might ... (probably something bad),” not “I don't understand”: 「何を言い出すか分かったものではない」 = there's no telling what he'll come out with.

daily.title: Complaining about a movie
daily.description: Grumbling to a friend about a really bad film.
daily.example: That movie is so bad it's unwatchable.

daily.title: Worrying about family
daily.description: Worrying that a careless family member will forget things again.
daily.example: If we leave it to that kid, who knows what'll be forgotten.

daily.title: A messy room
daily.description: Seeing a friend's dirty, cluttered room.
daily.example: With the place this messy, you can't possibly invite anyone over.

work.title: Judging a report
work.description: Privately criticizing a badly written report.
work.example: This report is full of typos. It's practically unreadable.

etymology: 「もの」 refers to the general nature of something, and 「〜ものではない」 denies it. Following the ta-form of a potential verb, it means “it's not something one can ...”, strongly denying any possibility.

similar.title: 〜ものではない
similar.explanation: Related. 「〜ものではない」 follows the dictionary form and means “one shouldn't ...” by common sense (「人を見た目で判断するものではない」), an admonition; 「〜たものではない」 follows the ta-form of a potential verb and means “simply can't ...,” a disparagement.

similar.title: 〜ようがない
similar.explanation: 「〜ようがない」 means you can't do something for lack of any way or means (「連絡先が分からないので、連絡しようがない」), an objective tone; 「〜たものではない」 means you can't ... because the thing is so bad, with strong subjective criticism.

similar.title: 〜っこない
similar.explanation: 「〜っこない」 is also a strong colloquial negation, but what it denies is possibility, “there's no way ...” (「勝てっこない」); 「〜たものではない」 focuses on judging the object as too poor to tolerate.

similar.title: 〜ものか・〜もんか
similar.explanation: Related; both use 「もの」 for strong negation. 「〜ものか」 expresses the speaker's resolve or rebuttal, “never ...” (「二度と行くものか」); 「〜たものではない」 is a disparaging evaluation of a thing.

formation: Built from the ta-form of a potential verb + the formal noun 「もの」 + the negative 「ではない」. 「もの」 sums up the nature of a thing, and 「〜られたものではない」 literally says “it is not the kind of thing that can be ...-ed,” directly denying that the thing is capable of being so treated. That is stronger than plain 「食べられない」, and it carries disparagement. The 「た」 rather than the dictionary form is generally thought to express confirmation or judgment: a verdict that “this thing is simply impossible to ....” Attached to 「分かる」 it becomes 「分かったものではない」, “there's no telling how it will turn out,” extended to worry about a bad outcome.

meaning: Follows the verb masu-stem: an action is half done, something is about to happen, or an action is directed at someone.
connection: Verb masu-stem + かける／かけだ／かけの + noun

senses.label: Half done
senses.meaning: An action has started but stopped partway: “half-...”, “started to ...”. 「〜かけの + noun」 means “a half-...ed ...”.
senses.connection: Volitional verb masu-stem + かける／かけた／かけの (読みかけ・食べかけ・書きかけ, etc.)
examples: There's a half-read book on the desk.
He started to say something, then stopped.
Don't throw away the half-eaten bread.

senses.label: About to / nearly
senses.meaning: With non-volitional verbs, a state is about to appear or nearly happened: “almost ...”, “nearly ...”. Common in 「死にかける」, 「忘れかける」 and 「消えかける」.
senses.connection: Non-volitional verb masu-stem + かける／かけている／かけた
examples: I once nearly died in an accident.
I remembered a dream I had almost forgotten.
The fire is about to go out.

senses.label: Directed at someone
senses.meaning: With verbs like 「話す」, 「呼ぶ」 and 「笑う」, the action is directed at someone: “to (speak, call, smile) to ...”. These have become set compound verbs.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + かける (話しかける・呼びかける・笑いかける・問いかける・働きかける)
examples: A stranger started talking to me.
The city is calling on residents to save electricity.

notes: After a volitional verb it mostly means “halfway through,” after a non-volitional verb mostly “almost ...”: 「死にかけた」 is “nearly died” (didn't), and 「言いかけてやめた」 is “stopped halfway through saying it.”
To modify a noun use 「〜かけの＋noun」: ✕「食べかけるパン」→ ○「食べかけのパン」.

For uses meaning “doing something toward someone,” such as 「話しかける」 and 「呼びかける」, the target takes 「に」: ✕「先生を話しかける」→ ○「先生に話しかける」. 「出かける」 and 「見かける」 are independent verbs and don't belong to this pattern.
「食べかけ」 and 「飲みかけ」 refer to something already partly eaten or drunk; handing someone half-eaten food is generally considered impolite in Japan, and you must never serve it to a guest.

daily.title: Tidying up
daily.description: A family member asks if they can throw something on the table away.
daily.example: I haven't finished drinking that, so don't throw it out yet.

daily.title: A close call
daily.description: Telling a friend about almost drowning.
daily.example: When I was a kid, I nearly drowned in a river.

daily.title: Meeting someone new
daily.description: Talking about being approached at the station.
daily.example: Someone from abroad came up to me at the station, so I gave them directions.

work.title: Handing over work
work.description: Before leaving, telling a coworker your work isn't finished.
work.example: There's a half-written email left in my drafts.

work.title: Government announcement
work.description: News reports the government's appeal to the public.
work.example: The government urged the public to evacuate early.

etymology: 「かける」 is written 「掛ける」 and originally means “to hang, to put on”. From “hooking onto an action, starting it” came “an action begun but unfinished”, and from “hanging an action on someone” came “directed at someone”.

similar.title: 〜かける・〜かけの
similar.explanation: Related: the same 「かける」 as the basic N3 explanation, focusing on “halfway / about to.” This entry additionally covers “directing toward someone” uses like 「話しかける」 and 「〜かけだ」 as a predicate.

similar.title: 〜途中で・〜途中に
similar.explanation: 「〜途中で」 means something happens at a point partway through a process or journey (「帰る途中で雨が降った」); 「〜かけ」 looks at the unfinished state of the action itself and often modifies a noun (「読みかけの本」).

similar.title: 〜そうになる
similar.explanation: 「〜そうになる」 means something almost happened but didn't (「転びそうになった」), mostly for involuntary events; 「〜かける」 can also mean this, but stresses that the change had already “started,” as in 「死にかけた」, which means you were once near death.

similar.title: 〜ところだった
similar.explanation: 「〜ところだった」 means “almost ... (luckily not),” where the event didn't happen at all (「遅れるところだった」); 「〜かけた」 means the change had already begun to occur in part.

formation: Built from the verb stem (ます-form) + the auxiliary verb 「かける」 (written 「掛ける」, “to hang, put on”). 「掛ける」 is “to put something on something,” hung up but not fully settled. After a verb it means “just put the action on, started it,” hence “halfway through.” After a verb of instant change such as 「死ぬ」 or 「倒れる」, “just touching on it” becomes “about to happen, almost happened.” On the other hand, 「掛ける」 also means “to direct ... at someone” (as in 「声を掛ける」), so 「話しかける」 and 「呼びかける」 mean directing the action at the other person. The noun form 「〜かけ」 fixes the “halfway” state, which is why you can say 「読みかけの本」.

meaning: Follows a Sino-Japanese noun: “from the standpoint of ...”, “in terms of ...”. Limits the angle or scope of a judgment.

senses.label: In terms of
senses.meaning: Judging from a certain angle or position: “in terms of ...”, “from a ... standpoint”. The second half is usually an evaluation like 「問題がある」 or 「好ましくない」.
senses.connection: Sino-Japanese noun + 上（は）、 + judgment (教育上・健康上・法律上・立場上・経験上・仕事上, etc.)
examples: Showing violent images to children is bad from an educational standpoint.
Given my position, I can't answer that question.
From experience, it's better not to panic at times like this.

senses.label: ...-related
senses.meaning: 「〜上の + noun」 modifies a noun: “...-related”, “for ... reasons”. 「健康上の理由」 means “health reasons”.
senses.connection: Sino-Japanese noun + 上の + noun (理由・問題・都合・ミス, etc.)
examples: I decided to leave the company for health reasons.
The service is down due to a system problem.

senses.label: On / within (a medium)
senses.meaning: After nouns for a medium or surface: “on ...”, “within ...”. 「ネット上」 is “online”, 「地図上」 is “on the map”.
senses.connection: Noun + 上で／上に／上の (ネット上・画面上・地図上・歴史上, etc.)
examples: Please don't post personal information online.
He studies historical figures.

notes: Read 「じょう」, not 「うえ」: 「教育上」 is 「きょういくじょう」, and 「立場上」 is 「たちばじょう」.
It attaches directly to a Sino-Japanese noun with no 「の」 between: ✕「教育の上よくない」→ ○「教育上よくない」. 「〜の上」 is read 「うえ」 and belongs to other patterns such as 「〜の上では」.
Different from 「〜的」: 「〜上」 means “from the standpoint of ...” and is followed by a judgment, while 「〜的」 describes a quality. ✕「健康上な食事」→ ○「健康的な食事」.
「立場上、お答えできません」 is a tactful way to decline; but saying only 「規則上できません」 to a client sounds blunt, so soften it with 「申し訳ございませんが」.

daily.title: A health program
daily.description: A doctor on TV explains the effects of a habit.
daily.example: Looking at your phone before bed isn't very good for your health.

daily.title: Online shopping
daily.description: Warning a friend about information online.
daily.example: You shouldn't believe every online review.

work.title: Declining to answer
work.description: Politely declining in a business setting by citing your position.
work.example: Given my position, I'm unable to share my personal opinion.

work.title: Legal consultation
work.description: A lawyer explains a legal problem with an approach.
work.example: This contract is legally problematic.

work.title: Explaining a process
work.description: Explaining that you'll organize things a certain way for convenience.
work.example: For convenience, I'll explain this in two groups: Team A and Team B.

etymology: 「上」 read 「じょう」 is the Sino-Japanese reading, from Chinese compounds like “in theory” and “in fact”. As a suffix after Sino-Japanese nouns, it marks an aspect or scope.

similar.title: 〜上で
similar.explanation: Related (both use 「上」). 「〜上で」 is read 「うえで」 and follows 「noun＋の」 or a verb, meaning “in the matter of ...” or “after ...” (「仕事の上で」, 「確認した上で」); 「〜上(じょう)」 attaches directly to a Sino-Japanese noun and is more concise and literary (「仕事上」).

similar.title: 〜の上では
similar.explanation: Related. 「〜の上では」 is read 「うえでは」 and often implies “on the surface, on paper it's so, but in reality it may differ” (「計算の上では間に合う」); 「〜上」 merely limits the viewpoint objectively, with no such contrast.

similar.title: 〜から見ると・〜からすると
similar.explanation: 「〜から見ると」 judges from a person's or position's viewpoint and can follow a person (「親から見ると」); 「〜上」 attaches only to Sino-Japanese nouns denoting a field and can't follow a person.

formation: Built from a Sino-Japanese noun + the on-reading suffix 「上(じょう)」. In Chinese, “... 上” already has the sense of “in terms of ...” (as in “in theory,” “in fact”), and Japanese borrowed the whole thing with the on-reading 「じょう」 as a word-forming suffix. 「noun＋上」 turns the noun into an “aspect, field or scope”; add 「は」 for an adverbial phrase (「教育上は」) or 「の」 to modify a noun (「健康上の理由」). Starting from “on a certain level,” it can limit the viewpoint of a judgment (立場上, 経験上) or indicate a space within some range (ネット上, 地図上); both extend from the “level” that 「上」 denotes.

meaning: States what parts or members make up a whole: “consists of ...”, “is made up of ...”.
connection: Noun + からなる／から成る／からなっている

senses.label: Consists of
senses.meaning: Objectively explains what elements or parts make up a whole: “consists of ...”. Mostly used to describe structure, number of members or components. Fairly formal.
senses.connection: Noun + からなる／からなっている／からなります
examples: Japan consists mainly of four large islands.
This committee is made up of ten experts.
Water consists of hydrogen and oxygen.

senses.label: Modifying a noun
senses.meaning: 「〜からなる + noun」 modifies a noun: “a ... consisting of ...”. Common in books, manuals and news.
senses.connection: Noun + からなる + noun (三部からなる小説・五人からなるチーム, etc.)
examples: This is a long novel in three parts.
A five-person team is running the project.

notes: In 「AはBからなる」, A is the whole and B the components; the order can't be reversed: ✕「四つの島は日本からなる」→ ○「日本は四つの島からなる」.
The particle decides the meaning: 「水は水素と酸素からなる」 is “water consists of hydrogen and oxygen,” while 「水が氷になる」 is “water turns into ice.” Swap 「から」 for 「に」 and it becomes “change.”
It is literary. In daily speech, what something is made of is usually 「〜でできている」; saying 「このケーキは卵と小麦粉からなる」 sounds like a product manual.

daily.title: Reading a manual
daily.description: Reading the structure of a product in its instructions.
daily.example: This set consists of three parts.

daily.title: At a museum
daily.description: A guide explains how the exhibition is organized.
daily.example: The exhibition is made up of five themes.

work.title: Company introduction
work.description: Explaining your company's structure to a client.
work.example: Our company consists of four divisions.

work.title: Academic report
work.description: Describing the structure of a questionnaire.
work.example: The questionnaire consists of twenty questions.

etymology: 「成る」 originally means “to be formed, to come into being”. 「から」 marks the source of the materials or elements. Together they mean “formed from ...”.

similar.title: 〜で作る・〜から作る（材料）
similar.explanation: 「〜でできている／〜からできている」 also says what something is made up of, is common in speech, and mostly names materials (「この家は木でできている」); 「〜からなる」 is more literary and mostly says a whole consists of so many parts or members (「三章からなる」, 「五人からなる」).

similar.title: 〜くなる・〜になる
similar.explanation: Related (the same verb 「なる(成る)」). 「〜になる」 means becoming some state (「医者になる」), while 「〜からなる」 means being composed of certain parts; the particle 「に」 or 「から」 decides whether it is “change” or “composition.”

formation: Built from the case particle 「から」 (starting point, source) + the verb 「成る(なる)」. 「成る」 originally means “to form, to be composed” (the 「成」 of 「成り立つ」 and 「完成」), and is the same word as the 「なる」 of change. 「から」 points to “where it comes from,” so 「Bから成る」 literally means “formed from these elements B”: B is the material or members, and the subject is the whole that is formed. Compared with 「AがBになる」 (A becomes B), 「から」 puts the focus on the source of the composition, so the pattern expresses structure rather than change.

meaning: Rather than do the first thing, which you really don't want to do, you'd prefer the second: “rather than ..., I'd sooner ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form + くらいなら／ぐらいなら + 〜ほうがいい／〜ほうがましだ

senses.label: I'd rather ...
senses.meaning: The speaker hates the idea of the first option so much they'd choose the second: “rather than ..., I'd sooner ...”. The second half is often 「〜ほうがましだ」 or 「〜ほうがいい」, sometimes with exaggeration.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + くらいなら、〜ほうがましだ／〜ほうがいい
examples: I'd sooner quit my job than bow down to someone like that.
Rather than ride a packed train, I'd prefer to walk for an hour.

senses.label: Advice / criticism
senses.meaning: Advising or criticizing someone: if you're going to do that, you'd be better off doing ... instead. The second half is often a command or suggestion.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + くらいなら、〜なさい／〜ばいい／〜ほうがいい
examples: If you're going to quit halfway, better not to start at all.
If you're going to regret it, apologize now while you can.
If you're going to complain, do it yourself.

notes: The first half is always what the speaker least wants, the second half the relatively acceptable option; swap them and the stance is reversed: 「頭を下げるくらいなら辞める」 is “I'd quit before bowing my head,” while 「辞めるくらいなら頭を下げる」 is “I'd bow my head before quitting.”
It follows the dictionary form of a verb; after a noun it becomes the degree usage: 「残業くらいなら平気だ」 means “if it's only overtime, that's fine,” not “rather than overtime ....”
The second half mostly uses 「〜ほうがいい」, 「〜ほうがましだ」 or advice, and is not used merely to state facts: ✕「雨に濡れるくらいなら、家にいた」→ ○「雨に濡れるくらいなら、家にいたほうがいい」.
It carries strong aversion; saying to someone 「あなたと行くくらいなら、一人で行く」 is deeply hurtful, and 「やめるくらいなら最初からやるな」 is also harsh and can't be used to a superior.

daily.title: Not wanting to wait in line
daily.description: A friend suggests a place with a long line, and you don't want to.
daily.example: Rather than wait two hours, let's go somewhere else.

daily.title: Advising a friend
daily.description: A friend complains about work but won't quit.
daily.example: If it's bothering you that much every day, why not change jobs?

work.title: Discussing a plan
work.description: Arguing in a meeting that redoing it is better than fixing it.
work.example: Rather than fix it, it'd be faster to rebuild it from scratch.

etymology: 「くらい」 was originally written 「位」 and indicates degree. 「〜くらいなら」 originally means “if it comes to the point of ...”, hence “rather than go that far, it's better to ...”.

similar.title: 〜ほうがましだ
similar.explanation: Often paired with 「〜くらいなら」, expressing “the lesser of two evils”; alone it just says the latter is relatively better (「歩いたほうがましだ」). 「〜くらいなら」 supplies the first half, the option you least want.

similar.title: 〜より(も)むしろ
similar.explanation: 「AよりむしろB」 is a calm comparison concluding B is more suitable, and A isn't necessarily bad; in 「AくらいならB」, A is an option the speaker finds extremely distasteful, with strong emotional coloring.

similar.title: 〜くらい・〜ぐらい（程度）
similar.explanation: Related. 「〜くらい」 (degree) simply expresses extent (「泣きたいくらい痛い」); adding 「なら」 makes it “if it comes to that point,” becoming an expression of choice. 「このくらいなら大丈夫」 means “if it's this much, it's fine,” which is the degree usage.

formation: Built from 「くらい(位)」, which expresses degree, + 「なら」, which expresses a supposition. 「くらい」 treats the first half as a “degree, extent,” and 「なら」 posits: “if it comes to that point ....” The speaker regards the first half as an extreme, unacceptable degree, and follows with 「〜ほうがましだ」, making a choice: “if I have to sink to that, I'd rather ....” Precisely because 「くらい」 originally expresses degree, the first half carries a tone of distaste, “to go as far as that.”

meaning: After comparing two things, the second is judged more fitting or more true: “rather than ..., (it's actually) ...”.
connection: Noun／Verb dictionary form + より（も）むしろ

senses.label: B is more fitting
senses.meaning: Comparing A and B, the speaker feels B is more appropriate or closer to the truth: “rather than A, B”, “more B than A”. Often combined with 「〜というより」.
senses.connection: A + より（も）むしろ + B (「〜というよりむしろ」 is also very common)
examples: I'd actually rather live in the countryside than in the city.
For contacting me, I'd much prefer email to a phone call.
This dish is spicy, if anything, rather than sweet.

senses.label: Contrary to expectations
senses.meaning: Reality runs against what one would normally expect: B is what's actually true. 「むしろ」 stresses “on the contrary”, “if anything”.
senses.connection: A + より（は）むしろ + B (B goes against common sense or expectations)
examples: His words sounded more like sarcasm than comfort.
Failure is not so much something shameful as a chance to grow.

notes: What precedes 「より」 is the side being outranked, and what follows 「むしろ」 is the speaker's conclusion; read what comes after 「むしろ」, or you will understand the speaker's stance backwards.
「むしろ」 implies “contrary to what is generally expected” and isn't used for a plain objective comparison: ✕「兄より弟のほうがむしろ背が高い」 (if there is no expectation to speak of) → ○「兄より弟のほうが背が高い」.
Saying 「AよりむしろBのほうがいいと思います」 directly to a superior or client amounts to rejecting their proposal and sounds rather strong; affirm first, then offer 「Bという方法もあるかと存じます」.

daily.title: Talking about preferences
daily.description: A friend asks if you prefer summer or winter.
daily.example: I actually like winter better than summer.

daily.title: Discussing a movie
daily.description: Talking with a friend about a movie you just saw.
daily.example: That movie was more sad than scary.

work.title: Speaking in a meeting
work.description: Offering a view that differs from the majority.
work.example: Rather than cutting costs, we should think about how to increase sales.

work.title: Opinion piece
work.description: Commenting on the real effects of a policy.
work.example: Rather than solving problems, this system is creating new ones.

etymology: 「むしろ」 can be written 「寧ろ」 in kanji. It means “of the two, preferably the latter”, and is used together with 「より」, which marks the standard of comparison.

similar.title: 〜というより
similar.explanation: 「〜というより」 focuses on “rather than put it as A, it's more B,” correcting a wording or characterization (「涼しいというより寒い」); 「〜よりむしろ」 can correct wording and also express choice or preference. The two are often combined: 「〜というよりむしろ〜」.

similar.title: 〜より〜のほうが
similar.explanation: Related (both use the comparison particle 「より」). 「AよりBのほうが」 is a neutral, objective comparison; 「AよりむしろB」 carries a subjective judgment that goes “contrary to what is generally expected.”

similar.title: 〜くらいなら
similar.explanation: In 「〜くらいなら」, the first half is something the speaker utterly detests and the second half a reluctant choice; 「〜よりむしろ」 is a calm comparison and choice, and A is not necessarily bad.

formation: Built from 「より」, the case particle marking a standard of comparison, + the adverb 「むしろ(寧ろ)」. The character 「寧」 in Chinese has the sense of “rather,” and 「むしろ」 means “of the two, I'd rather take the latter.” 「より」 first sets out the compared side A, then 「むしろ」 tips the scale toward B, so the whole means “rather than A, it's more like B.” 「むしろ」 itself carries an “unexpected, contrary to common assumption” feel, so it is often used to overturn the usual view, as in 「慰めよりむしろ皮肉に聞こえた」.

meaning: A formal, old-fashioned version of 「〜なければならない」: “must ...”, “have to ...”.
connection: Verb nai-form (drop ない) + ねばならない (する → せねばならない)

senses.label: Must / obligation
senses.meaning: You must do something out of duty, responsibility or necessity: “must ...”. More formal and solemn than 「〜なければならない」. Common in speeches, essays and editorials.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ねばならない／ねばならぬ／ねばなりません
examples: Promises must be kept.
We must resolve this problem as soon as possible.
There are times when the truth must be told.

senses.label: Sentence-final 「〜ねば」
senses.meaning: Dropping 「ならない」 and ending with 「〜ねば」 expresses your own resolve: “I'd better ...”, “I've got to ...”. It sounds a little old-fashioned or playful and is used in speech too.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ねば。(そろそろ帰らねば／がんばらねば)
examples: Is it that late already? I'd better get going.
Tomorrow I really must get up early.

notes: 「する」 becomes 「せねばならない」, not ✕「しねばならない」; 「しねば」 sounds like 「死ねば」 (“if you die”) and causes a serious misunderstanding. 「来る」 becomes 「来ねば(こねば)」.
「〜ねば」 and 「〜ば」 differ by a mere 「ね」 yet mean opposite things: 「行けば」 is “if I go,” while 「行かねば」 is “if I don't go.”

It has a strong classical flavor; saying 「行かねばならない」 to a friend sounds exaggerated, like acting. In speeches and writing, though, it sounds solemn and forceful. In daily life use 「〜なきゃ」 or 「〜なければならない」.

daily.title: Psyching yourself up
daily.description: Telling yourself before an exam that you must work hard.
daily.example: If I want to pass, I've got to study harder.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A character in a novel makes up their mind.
daily.example: No matter what happens, I must protect her.

work.title: A president's address
work.description: Stressing responsibility on a formal occasion.
work.example: We must live up to our customers' trust.

work.title: Editorial
work.description: An editorial makes its case.
work.example: The government must give the public a full explanation.

etymology: 「ね」 is the conditional (izen) form of the classical negative auxiliary 「ず」. Adding 「ば」 gives “if not ...”, followed by 「ならない」 (“it won't do”): “if you don't ..., it won't do”. It has the same structure as 「〜なければならない」 but keeps the classical form.

similar.title: 〜なければならない
similar.explanation: Same structure, same meaning. 「〜なければならない」 is the standard modern form, usable in speech and writing; 「〜ねばならない」 is the classical form, used in writing, speeches or when deliberately solemn.

similar.title: 〜べきだ
similar.explanation: 「〜べきだ」 means “should” by reason or duty, with the speaker's own opinion (「約束は守るべきだ」); 「〜ねばならない」 stresses the necessity of “can't be otherwise,” a more compelling tone.

similar.title: 〜ざるを得ない
similar.explanation: 「〜ざるを得ない」 means “have no choice but to ...” under circumstances, with resignation; 「〜ねばならない」 is “must,” which can be an active resolve or duty, without a note of resignation.

similar.title: 〜ぬ（否定）
similar.explanation: Related: 「ね」 and 「ぬ」 are both conjugated forms of the classical negative auxiliary 「ず」. 「〜ぬ」 is used at the end of a sentence or before a noun (「知らぬ間に」), and in 「〜ねばならぬ」 both appear together.

formation: Built from the classical negative auxiliary 「ず」 in its hypothetical (ba-conjugation) form 「ね」 + the conjunctive particle 「ば」 + 「ならない」. 「ね＋ば」 corresponds to modern 「〜なければ」 (“if not ...”), and 「ならない」 means “won't do, is no good,” so together it is “if not ..., it's no good” = “must.” It has exactly the same double-negative structure (negative condition + negative result) as 「〜なければならない」, only the first half keeps the classical form, so it sounds literary and solemn. Because 「ね」 attaches to the irrealis stem of the verb, 「する」 takes the irrealis 「せ」, giving 「せねば」.

meaning: A formal version of 「〜かどうか」: “whether or not ...”. Presents two possibilities that need to be judged.
connection: Verb・adjective plain form／noun・な-adj. stem + か否か

senses.label: Whether or not
senses.meaning: Raises “whether ... or not” as a question: “whether or not ...”. Often works as a subject or object, followed by 「〜は」, 「〜を判断する」, 「〜が問題だ」, etc.
senses.connection: Plain form + か否か (nouns and な-adjectives attach directly: 「事実か否か」)
examples: Please decide for yourselves whether or not to take part.
We need to confirm whether or not that information is true.
Whether you passed or not will be announced next week.

senses.label: Regardless of whether
senses.meaning: 「〜か否かを問わず」 and 「〜か否かにかかわらず」 mean “regardless of whether ...”: the condition doesn't matter.
senses.connection: Plain form + か否かを問わず／か否かにかかわらず
examples: Anyone can apply, with or without experience.
Admission is free, whether or not you are a member.

notes: 「否」 is read 「いな」, and 「か否か」 as a whole is read 「かいなか」, not ✕「かひか」.
After nouns and na-adjectives, attach 「か否か」 or 「であるか否か」 directly, without 「だ」: ✕「事実だか否か」→ ○「事実か否か」「事実であるか否か」.
It already contains both “yes” and “no,” so don't stack them: ✕「参加するかしないか否か」→ ○「参加するか否か」 or 「参加するかしないか」.
It is literary and stiff; saying 「行くか否か決めて」 to a friend is very unnatural. In speech use 「〜かどうか」.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: The news reports on whether a policy will go ahead.
daily.example: All eyes are on the government's decision on whether to raise taxes.

daily.title: Reading signup rules
daily.description: Reading the application guidelines for an event.
daily.example: Anyone can join, regardless of experience.

work.title: Making a decision
work.description: A meeting discusses whether to push ahead with a project.
work.example: We will decide by next month whether or not to continue this project.

work.title: Academic paper
work.description: Stating the question a study will test.
work.example: This study examines whether or not this hypothesis is correct.

etymology: 「否」, read 「いな」, is an old word meaning “no”. 「〜か否か」 literally means “... or not”.

similar.title: 〜かどうか
similar.explanation: Same meaning. 「〜かどうか」 is the general form, usable in speech and writing; 「〜か否か」 is literary and common in official documents, news and papers.

similar.title: 〜か（間接疑問）
similar.explanation: The 「か」 of an indirect question can follow a sentence with a question word (「何時に来るか分からない」); 「〜か否か」 is only for yes-or-no questions and can't be used with a question word: ✕「誰が来るか否か」.

similar.title: 〜や否や／〜や
similar.explanation: Related (both use 「否」). 「〜や否や」 means “as soon as ...” (「ドアが開くや否や、飛び出した」) and has nothing to do with “whether”; the two look alike, so when reading check whether the preceding particle is 「か」 or 「や」.

formation: Built from the interrogative particle 「か」 + the classical negative word 「否(いな)」 + the interrogative particle 「か」. 「否」 simply means “no, not,” so 「Aか否か」 literally asks “is it A, or is it not?”, setting the affirmative and negative possibilities side by side. This is the same structure as Chinese-style “whether or not” and the colloquial 「〜か〜ないか」; the kanji 「否」 just compresses “is not” into a single character, which makes it concise and literary. The whole works as a noun-like interrogative clause, and can be followed by 「は」, 「を」, 「が」, or by 「を問わず」 and 「にかかわらず」.

meaning: Picks up from the previous situation: “even so, that doesn't mean ...”, “but then again ...”. Usually followed by a negative or something you can't do.
connection: Sentence。かといって + negative sentence; Sentence + し／が、かといって + negative sentence

senses.label: Starting a sentence
senses.meaning: At the start of a sentence, it accepts the previous fact but says the usual conclusion doesn't follow: “but then again, ... not ...”. Often followed by 「〜わけにもいかない」 or 「〜ない」. Shows you're caught in a dilemma.
senses.connection: Sentence。（そう）かといって、〜ない／〜わけにもいかない
examples: My job is tough right now. But then again, I can't just quit.
Eating out is expensive. Then again, I don't have time to cook every day.

senses.label: Mid-sentence
senses.meaning: 「〜し、かといって」 or 「〜が、かといって」 links two clauses in one sentence: neither option is good, and it's hard to choose.
senses.connection: Sentence + し／が、かといって + negative
examples: I'm not big on meat, but vegetables alone don't fill me up.
I disagree with his approach, but I don't have a better idea either.

notes: 「かといって」 picks up the previous sentence, and the second half is mostly negative or “that won't do either”: ✕「仕事は大変だ。かといって、辞める。」→ ○「かといって、辞めるわけにもいかない。」

It differs from 「〜からといって」 by only one 「ら」: 「からといって」 follows a reason and means “you can't just ... on that reason alone” (「安いからといって買いすぎる」); 「かといって」 stands alone and picks up the situation of the previous sentence. Mixing them up makes the sentence nonsensical.

It expresses the predicament of “neither way works,” mostly about your own situation; using it in response to a superior's or client's proposal (「かといって、それもどうかと…」) sounds like nitpicking, so use it with care.

daily.title: Housing dilemma
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about housing worries.
daily.example: Rent is expensive, but I don't have the money to buy a house either.

daily.title: On a diet
daily.description: You want to eat sweets but are afraid of gaining weight.
daily.example: I want to hold back on sweets. But then again, not eating any at all is tough.

work.title: Discussing staff shortages
work.description: Explaining a dilemma in a meeting.
work.example: We're short-staffed. But then again, we're not in a position to hire right away.

etymology: It's made from the question particle 「か」 + the quotative 「と」 + the te-form of 「言う」. It originally means “even if one says (or thinks) so”, hence “even so, that doesn't mean ...”.

similar.title: 〜からといって
similar.explanation: Similar in form, and both express a concessive turn. 「〜からといって」 follows a reason and means “you can't just ... on that reason alone” (「日本人だからといって敬語が完璧とは限らない」); 「かといって」 picks up the previous situation, meaning “but the other approach won't work either.”

similar.title: 〜といっても
similar.explanation: Related (both built from 「と言う」). 「〜といっても」 means “although ..., actually the degree is not that high,” correcting the listener's expectation (「料理ができるといっても、簡単なものだけだ」); 「かといって」 expresses being caught in a dilemma.

similar.title: 〜とはいえ
similar.explanation: 「〜とはいえ」 means “although ..., but,” is literary, and the second half isn't limited to negatives (「春とはいえ、まだ寒い」); in 「かといって」 the second half is mostly negative, expressing a dilemma.

formation: Built from the interrogative particle 「か」 + the quotative particle 「と」 + the te-form 「言って」 of 「言う」, generally thought to be 「そうかといって」 with 「そう」 dropped. 「そうか」 is “is that so? / in that case,” and 「と言って」 is “even saying that,” so the whole means “that said.” The first half grants the preceding situation, and the second half, brought out by 「て」, turns to “but it can't be ... either,” forming a concessive turn: “that said, nor ....” Because what follows the concession is “the other path doesn't work either,” the second half is naturally mostly negative.

meaning: Once something is done or a state is entered, it continues or is hard to change afterwards: “once ..., ...”.
connection: いったん／一旦 + verb ba-form／と／たら

senses.label: Once ..., hard to undo
senses.meaning: Once the first thing happens, the second continues or is hard to reverse: “once ..., ...”. The second half is often 「なかなか〜ない」 or 「〜てしまう」.
senses.connection: いったん + verb dictionary form + と／verb ba-form + lasting, hard-to-change result
examples: Once something becomes a habit, it's hard to quit.
Once you lose people's trust, it's hard to win it back.
Once this machine starts running, it takes time to stop it.

senses.label: Once ..., you should ...
senses.meaning: The second half is the speaker's will, request or advice: “now that you've started, you should ...”. 「いったん〜たら」 is common.
senses.connection: いったん + verb たら／ば + will・command・advice
examples: Once you start, see it through to the end.
Once you take something on, you should see it through responsibly.

notes: 「いったん」 alone often means “for now, first” (「いったん家に帰ります」, 「いったん保存してください」); when no conditional form follows to match it, it does not mean “once.”

The second half is a result that necessarily appears and persists once the condition holds, or an attitude to be kept up; it is not used for an accidental one-off event: ✕「いったん駅に着くと、雨が降ってきた」→ ○「駅に着くと、雨が降ってきた」.
「一旦」 is read 「いったん」, not ✕「いちたん」.

daily.title: Can't stop scrolling
daily.description: Complaining to a friend that you can't stop watching videos.
daily.example: Once I start watching videos, before I know it, it's the middle of the night.

daily.title: Encouraging a child
daily.description: A parent encourages their child to stick with an instrument.
daily.example: Now that you've started, let's keep it up for at least a year.

work.title: Explaining a contract
work.description: Telling a client that the contract can't be canceled once signed.
work.example: Once the contract is concluded, it cannot be canceled.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: Commenting on how serious environmental damage is.
work.example: Once nature is destroyed, it's hard to restore it.

etymology: 「いったん」 is written 「一旦」, a word borrowed from Chinese. It originally meant “one morning, a short time” and later came to mean “once (something happens)”. Combined with the conditionals 「ば・と・たら」, it stresses the consequences once the condition is met.

similar.title: 〜が最後／〜たら最後
similar.explanation: 「〜たら最後」 also means “once ..., (it's irreversible),” but takes only bad results and sounds exaggerated (「彼に話したら最後、みんなに知られる」); 「いったん〜ば」 allows good or bad results and can also lead to a demand.

similar.title: 〜からには
similar.explanation: 「〜からには」 means “since ..., then must ...,” and the second half is mostly duty or resolve (「引き受けたからには最後までやる」); 「いったん〜たら」 can express this too, but stresses “once you've started.”

similar.title: 〜上は
similar.explanation: 「〜上は」 is a more literary “since ..., then ...,” with a second half that must be duty or resolve (「契約した上は、守らなければならない」); 「いったん〜と・ば」 can also express the objective result that “once ..., it's hard to change.”

formation: Built from the adverb 「いったん(一旦)」 paired with a conditional form 「〜と／〜ば／〜たら」. 「一旦」 originally means “one morning,” extended to “once, a certain moment.” It first limits the first half to “happening even once,” and the conditional then leads to the consequence: “once ..., then ....” Because it stresses “just once,” the second half is naturally a result of “there's no going back, it keeps going,” or a demand that “now that it has begun, see it through.” Used alone, the adverb takes the sense of “once, for now,” which is why 「いったん休憩する」 (take a break for now) exists too.
